newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan slaps harsh penalties on DKB, Nomura.
newsitem.headline: Japan slaps harsh penalties on DKB, Nomura.

text.p: Japan on Wednesday imposed stiff penalties on two top financial firms over a racketeer payoff scandal as the high-profile affair ensnared another brokerage.
The penalties imposed on giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd were the harshest ever imposed in Japan for violations of securities or banking laws.

Among the penalties dealt by the Finance Ministry on Nomura were orders to suspend own-account stock dealing until the end of the year, to halt operations at one of its corporate divisions until December, and a suspension from public bond auctions and underwriting until the year-end.

Penalties against DKB, one of Japan's biggest banks, included orders to halt new domestic lending except for housing loans until the year-end, to refrain from new overseas business except lending and from opening new overseas branches and offices or new domestic branches until August 1998.

DKB was also prohibited from investment trust sales at its branches, making use of holding companies, or liquidating assets by new methods -- all activities due to be liberalised as part of Japan's "Big Bang" reforms -- until August 1998.
Both firms were ordered to draft plans to improve their in-house operations to prevent a recurrence of the scandal.

Analysts said the penalties were likely to hit Nomura's bottom line harder than DKB's in the current business year to March 1998 and some expressed fears that Nomura might never get back clients lost to foreign rivals due to the scandal.

As if to underline that possibility, electronics giant Hitachi Ltd said on Wednesday it was shifting management of its bond investments to foreign firms from Japanese institutions because of a lack of transparency in their practices.

Others analysts, however, said the mighty Nomura would start winning back customers soon after the penalty period was over and that both firms might ultimately benefit from the massive management shake-ups resulting from the scandal.

More troubling, perhaps, was Wednesday's news that Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd had also been entangled in the scandal, which is unfolding just as Japan begins its "Big Bang" reforms aimed at boosting competition in its stodgy financial sector.
Prosecutors on Wednesday raided Yamaichi in search of evidence of alleged payoffs to Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the Nomura-DKB scandal.
A government source told reporters that Yamaichi had "generally" admitted to illegally paying compensation for losses incurred by a corporate client linked to Koike.
Prosecutors told reporters they suspected Yamaichi had paid 79 million yen ($669,000) to Koike.

Domestic media said Yamaichi allegedly made the payments in 1995 to obtain Koike's help in ensuring that its annual shareholders' meeting went smoothly. Yamaichi said in a statement that it would cooperate with the investigation but would not comment on whether the allegations were true.

Authorities are keen to be seen as tough on such misdeeds as they push forward with deregulation, and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference that stern steps could be expected against Yamaichi once the probe was completed.

Domestic media also said on Wednesday that prosecutors appeared to have launched investigations into the other two of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd, in connection with the affair.
A Daiwa spokesman denied reports of illicit deals and Nikko said it did not think it had done any illegal transactions.
Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1983, but many companies have found it tough to cut off underworld ties.

Sokaiya buy shares in companies and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices. Alternatively, they are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.

The Finance Ministry, itself under fire for years because of what some regard as its lax supervision of the financial institutions under its wing, also promised on Wednesday to strengthen its inspection and supervision as part of financial system reform.
On Tuesday, the ministry said it had reprimanded two of its officials who conducted inspections of DKB for accepting favours from officials of the scandal-tainted firm.

The ministry said the acts had not affected the results of inspections -- which failed to uncover the sokaiya loans -- but added that it was necessary to maintain discipline so that inspections would not lose credibility. ($1=118 yen)
